L33: # NVIDIA and Oracle Expand NVIDIA Vera Rubin to Multi-Gigawatt Scale and Bring NVIDIA Vera CPU to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure
L34: 
L35: NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 and NVIDIA Vera CPUs Are Now Generally Available on OCI, with Plans to Introduce Rubin HGX NVL8 Systems to Help Organizations Accelerate Frontier Model Training, Improve Inference Efficiency and Scale Agentic Workloads
L36: 
L37: Oracle AI World, LAS VEGAS—Oct 27, 2026
L38: 
L39: 【12†Image: Oracle and NVIDIA】
L40: NVIDIA and Oracle today announced plans to expand 【3†Oracle Cloud Infrastructure】 (OCI) Superclusters with 【13†NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72†www.nvidia.com】 systems to multi-gigawatt scale, supporting growing customer demand for AI training, inference and agentic applications. Oracle and NVIDIA also expanded their AI infrastructure collaboration with the general availability of NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 and 【14†NVIDIA Vera CPUs†www.nvidia.com】 on OCI.
L41: The expanded collaboration gives customers infrastructure for both the GPU-intensive work of training and serving frontier models and the CPU-intensive tasks agents perform between model calls, including executing tools, testing code and retrieving data. Customers can scale CPU and GPU resources independently to match their workloads, helping reduce idle capacity and put more of their infrastructure to productive use.
L42: ## OCI Superclusters Help Organizations Bring Frontier AI to Market Faster at Multi-Gigawatt Scale
L43: 【15†OCI Superclusters】 combine NVIDIA NVL72 rack-scale systems, 【16†Oracle Acceleron】 networking with 【17†NVIDIA†www.nvidia.com】 【17†Spectrum-X†www.nvidia.com】 Ethernet networking featuring NVIDIA Spectrum-6 switches and NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs, and gigawatt-class power and cooling to train and serve the largest AI models. Each rack connects 72 GPUs through 【18†NVIDIA NVLink†www.nvidia.com】 scale-up networking, while OCI’s resilient, multiplanar network scales across hundreds of thousands of GPUs.
L44: The planned Vera Rubin expansion builds on OCI’s existing NVIDIA-powered infrastructure, including NVIDIA 【19†GB200†www.nvidia.com】 and 【20†GB300†www.nvidia.com】 NVL72 systems. NVIDIA’s common CUDA software foundation and continued software optimization help customers support evolving models and workloads across hardware generations. OCI also plans to introduce NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8, delivering eight Rubin GPUs connected through NVLink in an x86-based server configuration.
L45: The planned platform features two 64-core Intel Xeon 6 CPUs, 4 TB of DDR5 memory, and 6.4 Tbps of high-speed RDMA networking, providing a flexible deployment option for AI training, fine-tuning, and inference. HGX Rubin NVL8 enables customers to adopt next-generation Rubin GPU technology in a smaller eight-GPU configuration while maintaining compatibility with x86-based applications.
L46: This flexibility enables customers to adapt their AI infrastructure to different models and workloads as their needs evolve, using accelerated computing capacity across both training and inference to make better use of their infrastructure investments.
L47: 
L48: OpenAI has demonstrated how this infrastructure supports frontier AI. In Abilene, OpenAI has trained and served GPT-6 Astra on an OCI Supercluster with more than 100,000 【21†NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs†www.nvidia.com】.
L49: “As our frontier models advance, we need infrastructure that can keep pace,” said Sreekanth Pothanis, engineering leader, compute infra at OpenAI. “NVIDIA Vera Rubin on OCI gives us the computing performance and scale to accelerate model training and serve increasingly demanding AI workloads.”
L50: ## NVIDIA Vera CPUs on OCI Accelerate the Work Behind AI Agents
L51: 
L52: AI agents do more than generate responses. They call tools, execute code and retrieve information to complete tasks. Slow execution of those CPU-intensive operations can delay results and leave GPUs waiting between model calls.
L53: OCI Compute with NVIDIA Vera CPUs combines high single-thread performance with memory bandwidth to help agents complete CPU-intensive tasks faster. High single-thread performance accelerates individual tool calls and code execution, while high memory bandwidth keeps CPU cores supplied with data as agents run concurrent tasks. Together these capabilities help reduce GPU idle time and maintain consistent performance as workloads scale.
L54: To further support these workloads, OCI Kubernetes Engine enables customers to scale CPU and GPU resources independently, while Oracle Acceleron provides hardware-based isolation for workloads running untrusted, AI-generated code.
L55: Customers with early access to NVIDIA Vera CPUs on OCI, including OpenAI, are exploring their potential across a range of AI workloads:
L56: 
L57: “NVIDIA Vera CPUs on OCI deliver the world-class loaded performance needed to execute code and run tools across our rapidly growing agentic sandbox workloads,” said Uday Ruddarraju, chief technology officer of compute at OpenAI. “We are bringing Vera into production on OCI to support these workloads at scale.”
L58: “Oracle Cloud Infrastructure gives customers the performance, security and scale to advance frontier AI,” said Mahesh Thiagarajan, president of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, Oracle. “Our collaboration with NVIDIA extends those capabilities across training, inference and agentic AI. By combining NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs with Oracle Acceleron networking and AI-optimized data centers, we’re helping customers keep GPUs productive, secure, and scale efficiently as their needs grow.”
L59: “AI factories must be productive, durable and fungible—delivering efficient computing, remaining useful through continued software advances and serving different models and workloads as demand changes,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “With Oracle, we’re bringing Vera Rubin and Vera CPUs to OCI to help customers put more of their infrastructure to work today and sustain its value as AI evolves.”

L665: Hi, everyone. Welcome back to the final sessions of today's Investor Day. In fact, just myself, and then we'll go straight to the Q&A. Great to have everyone joining us here, both in person and also thanks for joining via the webcast. You've heard from Mike and a number of my colleagues here today about the really amazing things that Oracle is doing with technology enhanced by AI to create value. I'm going to put that into further perspective on how it creates value for our shareholders.
L666: At Oracle, we are very simply the right company at the right time to take advantage of this wave of intelligence driven by AI. We announced that vision and strategy last year.
L667: Now we're a year into the journey and ready to share with you, with confidence, what that looks like from our P&L to our balance sheet between now and 2030. It all starts with differentiated growth. You can already see in our guidance for fiscal 2027 a +34% growth rate year-over-year. That path continues to 2030, where we expect to be at $225 billion plus in revenues. Of course, profitability and free cash flows are equally important drivers of value creation.
L668: We're happy to share with you today our path to free cash flow positive sometime during the second half of our fiscal 2028 and to $30 billion plus in free cash flows in our fiscal 2029. I'll also speak through our margin expectations for the company as we undertake this significant transformation.
L669: In terms of disciplined capital allocation, we have done significant work on our funding journey over the past months. I've told you we need an additional up to $20 billion in funding for the remainder of our fiscal 2027. We're announcing that this $20 billion, split evenly between debt and equity, is the final amount needed to fund the remainder of this cycle. Let me dive into the details, starting with differentiated growth.
L670: Mike said at the beginning of his presentation that AI is the catalyst that makes every part of our portfolio more valuable. This is translating into a growth opportunity for us that's truly differentiated for a company of our size. In infrastructure, demand remains extremely robust, both for short-term and longer-term capacity.
L671: Our RPO at $664 billion is one of the largest in the industry, with more than 90% of that tied to our infrastructure business. In AI infrastructure, we were a first mover in the market, building a significant RPO with a single customer in our fiscal 2026, and we have continued to grow our RPO quarterly since. With those additions, we have diversified our RPO each quarter.
L672: In applications, you saw with Chris and Simon the opportunities to continue to grow our subscription revenue with both current and new customers, as well as exciting new opportunities for AI consumption revenue and on-top revenue opportunities like embedded finance. In database, AI is driving more data and usage, while availability through multi-cloud expands our market and accelerates growth.
L673: Our portfolio positioning and strategic choices mean our total addressable market is positioned to grow at CAGRs of greater than 20%, and we are positioned to grow far faster than that over the next years. What gives us confidence in that differentiated growth in our portfolio? First, in this slide, we have depicted the flywheel we see accelerating our business today, and we talked a lot about that throughout the sessions already.
L674: We have always been a company that drives measurable customer outcomes, and with AI, it becomes even faster to show proof points of strong outcomes that encourage broader adoption across customer portfolios. This, in turn, drives more demand for cloud database, data services, and for compute itself. There are very few companies that can claim this reinforcing flywheel across our portfolio, supporting a path to differentiated growth.
L675: Another point giving us confidence is more of our contracted revenues are now tied to projects already under construction. Mahesh shared with you earlier today how we differentiate in infrastructure, including in execution, and we continue to be confident in the plans we have to deliver around 7 GW incremental capacity over the next couple of years. This will put us with a portfolio of around 10 GW at the end of our fiscal 2028.
L676: This acceleration in capacity delivery to support contracted RPO leads us to a period of peak CapEx in fiscal 2027 and 2028, with our CapEx stepping down in fiscal 2029. We will continue to grow our business in fiscal 2029 and beyond.
L677: In fact, these around 7 GW in projects ramp into strong free cash flow contributors fairly quickly, meaning we will be in a position to both be free cash flow positive again sometime during our second half of our fiscal 2028, and to self-fund the growth of our business starting in fiscal 2029. I will get into some more detail on our cash flow and capital planning in a few minutes. One point to note is our large sites are only driving a part of that contribution.
L678: The five large-scale sites we have underway account for around 5 GW in total capacity to be delivered between our fiscal 2026 and mid-fiscal 2029. Each of these sites is plus or minus a few hundred megawatts from 1 GW, and one of those sites, Abilene, is already nearing completion today.
L679: Our strong confidence in that path to differentiated growth underpins the revenue commitments we are making today of $225 billion plus in our fiscal 2030. That is a 35% CAGR and an addition of $158 billion plus over four years. As we ramp up our projects, we expect to see reasonably consistent revenue growth across our fiscal 2028 and fiscal 2029. Of course, differentiated growth alone is not enough to drive acceleration in value creation.
L680: Profitability, free cash flows, and return on investment are also key drivers. We have a transformation underway at Oracle, not just in technology, but across our business models. The new technology backbone being created with AI infrastructure is driving different growth rates between our different business models over this cycle. It is important to understand that when you think about our profitability over the next years.
L681: In our cloud applications or SaaS business, we expect to continue to drive double-digit growth with low capital intensity, very high gross margins, and relatively high operating costs in the form of R&D and sales. Cloud database will have very high growth, well in excess of 50%, and moderate capital intensity. Similar to SaaS, cloud database has very high gross margins and relatively high operating expenses as a percentage of sales.
L682: Our infrastructure business is a very different business model with relatively lower gross margins and high capital intensity. However, it also has relatively lower operating expenses as a percentage of sales, particularly when supported by the networking technology differentiation that Oracle has already created and continues to create in its database business. There is a big differential in gross margin between these business models.
L683: However, at the level of operating margin, this differential closes quite a bit.
L684: All three of our business models contribute strongly to our profitable growth journey. Historically, our non-GAAP operating margin has trended in the lower 40s percent. We show here in fiscal 2026, it was 43%. We do anticipate some near-term margin pressure from mix, as well as the ramp-up of our projects over the next few years. However, with the continued strong contribution from our apps and database businesses and focused cost management, we will be back at a 40%+ margin in fiscal 2030.
L685: At the peak of our ramp-up impacts, that is in fiscal 2028 and fiscal 2029, we are not significantly below that. To dive a bit deeper into the contributions from apps and database, there are a couple of points I would like to draw out from these slides. First, on apps. Chris covered the evolution of our pricing models with the addition of outcome-based pricing.
L686: We continue the journey made faster by AI to migrate customers to the cloud. That results in, Simon said 3x, I think it is 3x-4x , a 4x pricing uplift versus on-prem. In database, AI is driving a shift to higher value database services. We continue to scale our multi-cloud business, and AI Data Platform offers another great opportunity to expand our monetization models as customers focus on using intelligence to drive results.
L687: We have received a lot of questions about our infrastructure business model, so we thought it would be helpful to provide a 1 GW example for education and modeling purposes. This is roughly reflective of the economics of our next few years of projects, and this is, of course, based on Oracle's business model for data centers. So it assumes we are leasing the shell, the power, et cetera. A few things to call out here.
L688: Each of our five large sites is planned at plus or minus a few hundred megawatts from 1 GW. This is a good proxy for each of those sites. One of those sites is close to fully executed, Abilene. We have four sites expected to start first service delivery in calendar 2027. Of course, our financial guidance takes into account up to a couple of quarters delay on any of those. Mahesh highlighted those sites are not built as a single project.
L689: In fact, they roll out as a series of data halls and buildings over time. As a result, the lease obligations, CapEx commitments, and revenues ramp up as the build progresses. This means, in the case of a delay, most of the costs are delayed as well. Plus, a lot of the hardware is fungible site by site.
L690: We have also given the details on average project-level economics reflective of our current RPO. CapEx at around $37 billion is a bit less than 50% of total contract value. Revenues are around $16 billion per gigawatt annualized, so that is once we ramp up. While our gross margin is at around 35%, operating margin at the project level is around 34% due to that OpEx-light business model I described earlier. This business model generates strong free cash flow fairly quickly as we ramp up.
L691: Fully ramped, a 1 GW project will convert 100% of its non-operating profit after tax plus depreciation into cash flows annually. I have spoken about our returns on investment in the high 20s in the past. Here you can see the details of the calculation itself.
L692: We have added back depreciation in the numerator because this business has limited maintenance CapEx, aside from new IT equipment, around when we would expect to recontract or later. Please note, effectively, all of our large AI infrastructure contracts are cost plus or similar. So revenues may change, but the margin and ROI will remain. As we demonstrated in our prior slide, this is overall a very attractive business model, albeit capital intense when self-funded.
L693: In the model shown on this slide, we pay for all $37 billion of the required CapEx in the first two years of the project. We have been looking at some models to reduce that capital intensity, and we show the directional impacts of those in the next couple of slides. One key lever we are availing of is vendor financing.
L694: We have strong partners on the supply side who are willing to support us, and you can see an illustrative example here of a simple 70% five-year vendor financing. This reduces the capital needed from Oracle in the first two years to $18 billion, a 50% decrease. Bring your own hardware is where a customer provides their preferred chipset to us, reducing our capital requirements to a minimal $6 billion or lower. Again, based on this 1 GW example.
L695: Of course, with bring your own hardware, there is some impact to the project economics with lower revenues and higher margins. Mahesh talked through the value add to our customers in that scenario. This slide summarizes the simple examples I just walked through. In the case of self-funding and vendor financing, the total level of CapEx and project economics remain roughly the same.
L696: What changes is the timing of our capital needs, with vendor financing shifting those payments to be better aligned with our revenue ramp. Bring your own hardware changes the capital intensity of the project itself, driving higher margins and higher returns on investment. I will close this section with a few further points of guidance.
L697: Based on the strength of our three business models, including the strong cash conversion from our infrastructure projects I described a few minutes ago, we expect to drive greater than $30 billion in free cash flow in fiscal 2029. I mentioned the 40%+ operating margin we expect in fiscal 2030, and we also anticipate $21+ in non-GAAP EPS. Of course, there is a question of recontracting and the necessity for the renewal of GPUs at the end of our various contracts.

L35: ## Oracle Unveils Next-Generation Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Zettascale10 Cluster for AI
L36: 
L37: Largest AI supercomputer in the cloud delivers 10X the amount of zettaFLOPS of peak performance
L38: 
L39: Built on Oracle Acceleron RoCE networking architecture with NVIDIA AI infrastructure, OCI Zettascale10 will provide multi‑gigawatt AI workload capacity and scale
L40: 
L41: Oracle AI World, Las Vegas—Oct 14, 2025
L42: 
L43:   * 【14†Facebook】
L44:   * 【14†Twitter】
L45:   * 【14†LinkedIn】
L46:   * 【14†Email】

L48: 【15†Image: OCI Zettascale10】
L49: Oracle today announced 【3†Oracle Cloud Infrastructure】 (OCI) Zettascale10, the largest AI supercomputer in the cloud. OCI Zettascale10 connects hundreds of thousands of NVIDIA GPUs across multiple data centers to form multi-gigawatt clusters that deliver up to an unprecedented 16 zettaFLOPS of peak performance. OCI Zettascale10 is the fabric underpinning the flagship supercluster built in collaboration with OpenAI in Abilene, Texas, as part of Stargate.
L50: Built on next-generation Oracle Acceleron RoCE networking architecture, OCI Zettascale10 is powered by NVIDIA AI infrastructure that delivers breakthrough scale, extremely low GPU-GPU latency across the cluster, industry-leading price-performance, improved cluster utilization, and the reliability required for large scale AI workloads.
L51: OCI Zettascale10 is a powerful evolution of the first Zettascale cloud computing cluster, which was introduced 【16†in September 2024】. OCI Zettascale10 clusters are housed in large gigawatt data center campuses that are hyper-optimized for density within a two-kilometer radius to offer the best GPU-GPU latency for large scale AI training workloads. This architecture is being deployed with OpenAI at the Stargate site in Abilene.
L52: “With OCI Zettascale10, we’re fusing OCI’s groundbreaking Oracle Acceleron RoCE network architecture with next-generation NVIDIA AI infrastructure to deliver multi‑gigawatt AI capacity at unmatched scale,” said Mahesh Thiagarajan, executive vice president, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. “Customers can build, train, and deploy their largest AI models into production using less power per unit of performance and achieving high reliability.
L53: In addition, customers will have the freedom to operate across Oracle’s distributed cloud with strong data and AI sovereignty controls.”
L54: “OCI Zettascale10 network and cluster fabric was developed and deployed first at the flagship Stargate site in Abilene, Texas – our joint supercluster with Oracle,” said Peter Hoeschele, vice president, Infrastructure and Industrial Compute, OpenAI. “The highly scalable custom RoCE design maximizes fabric-wide performance at gigawatt scale while keeping most of the power focused on compute. We’re excited to keep scaling Abilene and the broader Stargate program together.”
L55: OCI plans to offer multi-gigawatt deployments of OCI Zettascale10 to customers. Initially, OCI Zettascale10 clusters will target deployments of up to 800,000 NVIDIA GPUs delivering predictable performance and strong cost efficiency, with high GPU‑to‑GPU bandwidth enabled by Oracle Acceleron’s ultra‑low‑latency RoCEv2 networking.
L56: “Oracle and NVIDIA are bringing together OCI’s distributed cloud and our full‑stack AI infrastructure to deliver AI at extraordinary scale,” said Ian Buck, vice president of Hyperscale, NVIDIA. “Featuring NVIDIA full-stack AI infrastructure, OCI Zettascale10 provides the compute fabric needed to advance state‑of‑the‑art AI research and help organizations everywhere move from experimentation to industrialized AI.”
L57: ## Oracle Acceleron RoCE networking delivers scale, reliability, and efficiency for AI on OCI Zettascale10
L58: Oracle Acceleron RoCE networking architecture is a critical innovation for customers to build, train, and inference AI workloads in the cloud, while taking full advantage of OCI Zettascale10’s power and capabilities. It uses the switching capability built into modern GPU 【17†NICs†www.nvidia.com】 (network interface cards), allowing them to connect to multiple switches simultaneously, with each on a separate and isolated network plane.
L59: This approach dramatically increases the network’s overall scale and reliability by shifting traffic to other network planes when one has a problem, avoiding costly stalls and restarts. Key features of Oracle Acceleron RoCE networking that help customers with their critical AI workloads, include:
L60:   * Wide, shallow, resilient fabric: Helps customers deploy larger AI clusters faster at lower total cost by using the GPU NIC as a mini‑switch and connecting to multiple physically and logically isolated planes. This boosts scale while reducing network tiers, cost, and power.
L61:   * Higher reliability: Helps customers maintain the stability of AI jobs by eliminating data sharing across planes. This shifts traffic away from unstable or congested planes, which keeps training jobs running and avoids costly checkpoint restarts.
L62:   * Consistent performance: Provides customers with more uniform GPU‑to‑GPU latency by removing a tier versus traditional three-tier designs, improving predictability for large‑scale AI training and inference.
L63:   * Power‑efficient optics: Supports customer workloads with Linear Pluggable Optics (LPO) and Linear Receiver Optics (LRO) to cut network and cooling costs without sacrificing 400G/800G throughput. This allows customers to devote more of their power budget to compute.
L64:   * Operational flexibility: Helps customers reduce downtime and speed up feature rollouts through plane‑level maintenance and independent network operating system updates.
